newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks "honorable compromise" on budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks "honorable compromise" on budget.

text.p: President Bill Clinton unveiled his new federal budget on Thursday and said he seeks an "honorable compromise" with Congress to eliminate deficits, but Republicans gave the proposal a decidedly cool reception.

Clinton's $1.69 trillion fiscal 1998 budget proposed $98.4 billion in tax cuts over five years offset in part by $76 billion in higher taxes. It shows the deficit gradually narrowing over four years, with a surplus in 2002.
In presenting the budget, Clinton, a Democrat, acknowleged there were differences between himself and the Republicans who control both the Senate and the House of Representatives.

"I am convinced those differences can be bridged," Clinton told a news conference. "Some of the differences we have are truly principled differences and we will have to work hard to have an honourable compromise but I believe that we can do it."

Stalemates over the budget led to two brief partial shutdowns of federal government operations in late 1995 and early 1996. Many Americans blamed that more on the Republicans than on Clinton, a develpment that has led Republican leaders to sound more conciliatory themselves this time around.

The fiscal 1998 budget, which covers the year beginning on Oct. 1, forecast that the 1998 deficit would narrow to $120.6 billion from 1997's $125.6 billion and gradually shrink over the next three years to become a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
In putting the proposal forward, Clinton was essentially presenting his opening offer in the annual budget negotiations between the White House and the Republican-held Congress.
In responding, the Republicans were less harsh than in years past, when they routinely pronounced the president's budget "dead on arrival." Still, their reception was cool.

"As for the whole budget, well, I suppose that you could say it's alive, but definitely not kicking," said Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican who will be one of the party's key negotiators on this issue.
The mere fact that the Republicans did not immediately condemn Clinton's budget outright appeared a positive sign, despite the fact that several of them found faults with it.

"We just really do not have the kind of bold document that we would like to see that would be a message to people that there really is change in Washington," said Representative John Kasich, an Ohio Republican who chairs the House Budget Committee.
Speaking at a news conference, Kasich challenged Clinton's key balanced-budget prediction, saying bluntly: "It does not balance in the year 2002."

Sen. Pete Domenici, the New Mexico Republican who chairs the Senate Budget Committee, went further, saying he expected the plan would be $50 billion in deficit in 2002 using the economic assumptions of the Congressional Budget Office.
The two Republicans mixed their criticisms with slightly more conciliatory assessments, with Domenici suggesting he believed compromises could be worked out between the parties.

"I do not think this budget is dead on arrival," Domenici said. "We are going to have to do a lot of working together to bridge the gap that is clear between that (Clinton) budget and what we feel will be good for the future of our country."

Overall, the Republicans want a larger and broader tax cut than Clinton advocates, as well as a more dramatic effort to rein in entitlements like the Medicare and Medicaid health care programmes for the elderly and the poor.

Clinton's proposed $98.4 billion in tax cuts included a $500 per child credit, a $1,500 tax credit or $10,000 tax deduction for college tuition, and an extension of the capital gains tax exclusion on home sales to $500,000 per couple.

At the same time, the budget proposed raising $34.3 billion by closing corporate tax loopholes and extending expiring excise and other taxes worth $41.7 billion, leading to such tax revenue increases of $76 billion over five years.
It would also raise $36.1 billion from sales of broadcast spectrum licenses to private industry over the five years.
As previously reported, the budget would trim $100 billion over five years from projected spending on the politically sensitive Medicare health care programme for the elderly.
Wall Street economists and traders criticised some of the budget's economic assumptions, and said they had heard promises of balancing the budget before.

"We've been hearing the balanced budget speech forever," said Daiwa Securities trader Joseph Benning. "The market's attitude is: 'Show me.' We've heard this song so many times before, it's just not worth going through the drill again."
